title: How Do Pigeons Fly 600 Miles Home?
description:
Homing pigeons can find their loft from hundreds of miles away using a sun compass, a magnetic sense on cloudy days, a smell map carried on the wind, and roads and landmarks for the last few miles. We look at William Keeton's clock-shift trick that sent pigeons 90 degrees off course, the tiny magnets that got them lost under clouds, the Oxford GPS study that caught pigeons following highways and roundabouts, and how fast racing pigeons really fly.

Sources:
https://digfir-published.macmillanusa.com/hlw/hlw_ch45_5.html
https://theconversation.com/explainer-how-do-homing-pigeons-navigate-25633
https://www.earthdate.org/episodes/homing-pigeons

Animated in the Synthwave Outrun style.

topic: How do homing pigeons find their way home from hundreds of miles away?
script:
Take a pigeon six hundred miles from home and let it go.
It'll be back the same day.
No map, no phone, no GPS.
And nobody fully knows how it does it.
So how does a bird that small know the way?
Let's take a ride along its route.
People figured out this trick a long time ago.
The ancient Egyptians and Romans carried pigeons on trips
and let them go with messages.
Back in 44 BC, a Roman general sent his notes by pigeon.
Here's the secret.
Any pigeon can find its own home.
Breeders just start them young,
with short practice flights from a mile or two away,
then farther and farther.
Scientists think a pigeon needs two tools.
A compass, to tell which way is which.
And a map, to know where home actually is.
Let's start with the compass.
On a sunny day, a pigeon steers by the sun.
But the sun moves fifteen degrees every hour,
so the bird has to know what time it is.
Decades ago, a scientist named William Keeton played a sneaky trick.
He kept pigeons under lamps that ran six hours off.
Then he let them go on a sunny day.
Home was west,
but the birds flew north.
They were off by ninety degrees,
exactly what a six-hour mistake would cause.
So the sun really is their compass.
But what about cloudy days?
Pigeons still get home.
Keeton tried tiny magnets on their backs.
In sunshine, the magnets did nothing.
Under clouds, those birds got lost.
So pigeons have a backup.
They can feel Earth's magnetic field.
A compass is great,
but it's useless if you don't know where home is.
So where's the map?
Many scientists think it's up the pigeon's nose.
Pigeons that can't smell
get lost when they're released somewhere new.
The idea is that every region has its own mix of smells,
carried along by the wind.
A young pigeon sitting in its loft
learns which smells blow in from which direction.
Smell the forest, and home is that way.
Some researchers think pigeons might also hear
super-low sounds that travel for miles,
but that's still being tested.
Now here's the funniest part.
Close to home, pigeons switch to their eyes.
Oxford scientists put tiny GPS trackers on pigeons.
And the birds followed the roads.
They flew straight down a highway,
turned at the traffic lights,
and even went around a roundabout.
It's easier than thinking, so they just follow the road.
So how good are they?
A racing pigeon averages about fifty miles an hour.
With a tailwind, it can hit ninety.
Some races run six hundred miles,
and the longest have gone over a thousand miles.
Sun for the compass.
Magnetism when it's cloudy.
Smell for the map.
And roads for the last few miles.
Four senses, one tiny brain, and it still beats your phone's battery.
Next time, your bones are alive.
So how do they rebuild themselves?
key_facts: Racing pigeons average about 50 mph over typical race distances, up to 85-90 mph with a tailwind (EarthDate; WCCO/CBS Minnesota)
Races commonly run up to about 600 miles; the longest races are around 1,100 miles (CBS Minnesota; EarthDate)
Pigeons were used as messengers in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome; pigeon post was used at the siege of Modena in 44 BC (EarthDate)
Young birds are trained with short releases that get gradually farther from the loft
The sun moves about 15 degrees an hour; a 6-hour clock shift sends pigeons about 90 degrees off (Keeton 1969; textbook ch. 45.4)
Pigeons wearing magnets home fine on sunny days but fail on cloudy days (Keeton; textbook ch. 45.4)
Pigeons that cannot smell cannot navigate from unfamiliar places; the map is thought to be olfactory, built from wind-borne odours (The Conversation; Wallraff 2013 via ScienceDaily)
Infrasound has been proposed as a cue but has little support so far (The Conversation; EarthDate)
Oxford GPS tracking (Guilford) showed pigeons following roads such as the A34, turning at traffic lights and going around roundabouts (AFP via Al Jazeera, 2004)
